sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: On-policy distillation can transfer the reasoning capabilities of a strong teacher to a smaller student. However, distillation from a stronger teacher model faces two mismatches: its solutions may be difficult for a smaller student to imitate, and its token-level probabilities may be incompatible with, or even unavailable to, the student. Existing methods handle these settings through different forms of supervision. To this end, we propose Bridged Self-Distillation (BSD), a unified framework for distilling from any teacher that provides reasoning traces. The model to be distilled from, termed the external teacher, first provides a reasoning trace as privileged context, which can be generated in an offline fashion. The student generates rollouts without this context, while a copy of the student conditioned on it, serving as the self-teacher, scores the same rollouts in the student's own token space. BSD uses the resulting token-level guidance to adjust updates on unsuccessful rollouts, with a verifier providing the outcome signal. As the external teacher is queried only to produce text, the same training procedure applies to all teacher scenarios: shared-tokenizer, cross-tokenizer, and closed API teachers. Across these scenarios, BSD improves over the base model and outperforms baselines tailored to each scenario, offering a novel and unified pathway for distillation. Code is available: https://github.com/TUMLegalTech/Bridged-Self-Distillation

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large reasoning models have become increasingly capable on tasks that require multi-step reasoning (Wei et al., 2022; Ahn et al., 2024; Muennighoff et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025). Much of *Equal contribution. Corresponding author. 1 Figure 1: Comparison between scenario-specific OPD and BSD. Top: existing methods derive different training signal for each kind of teacher access, namely tokenlevel distribution matching with shared tokenizer, vocabulary mapping across tokenizers, and response-based feedback for closed API. Bottom: BSD uses unified framework for all three scenarios: the external teacher provides reasoning trace z, and self-teacher conditioned on scores the students own on-policy rollouts. this progress comes from post-training, typically including supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on reasoning traces and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) (Ouyang et al., 2022; Chung et al., 2024; Shao et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2025a,b; Yu et al., 2025). Yet the cost of running large reasoning model makes it desirable to transfer its capabilities to smaller student models that can respond more quickly and be deployed more widely (Hinton et al., 2015; Kim and Rush, 2016). On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as promising post-training approach for this purpose, allowing smaller model to learn from the guidance of stronger teacher (Gu et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2024; Ko et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025; Lu and Lab, 2025; Li et al., 2026b; Song and Zheng, 2026). In standard OPD, the student generates its own rollouts, and the teacher scores the students tokens to guide training (Ross et al., 2011; Agarwal et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026). This requires access to the teachers next-token distributions and way to align them with the students tokenization. However, when teacher and student use different tokenizers, these distributions cannot be compared directly; when the teacher is available only through closed API, they may be inaccessible. Cross-tokenizer OPD methods address the former by constructing mappings between the token spaces of the student and teacher (Zhang et al., 2024; Minixhofer et al., 2025; Boizard et al., 2025; Niu et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026), while blackbox methods address the latter using feedback such as rubrics or sampled continuations (Jiang et al., 2023; Ye et al., 2026a; Fang et al., 2026; Xiong et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026). These methods expand the range of usable teachers, but require different training signals for different teacher settings (Figure 1, top). Alternatively, SFT can train on teacher-generated text without accessing probabilities, although directly imitating much stronger models reasoning can be difficult for small student (Zhang et al., 2023, 2025; Huang et al., 2026; Lyu et al., 2026). This motivates unified on-policy learning method that can distill from any teacher capable of providing reasoning traces. We propose Bridged Self-Distillation (BSD) to turn the reasoning of an external teacher into guidance on the students own rollouts (Figure 1, bottom). The external teacher is the model we aim to distill from, and BSD requires only its reasoning trace. Instead of training the student to imitate the teachers solution, as in SFT, we provide that solution as privileged context to copy of the student. Inspired by on-policy self-distillation (Zhao et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a), this conditioned copy serves as self-teacher, scoring rollouts generated by the student without the privileged context. Both versions score the same tokens in the students own token space, and the differences show how access to the teachers reasoning changes the students predictions along its rollouts. BSD uses these differences to adjust token-level penalties on unsuccessful rollouts, while verifier determines the direction of the updates. Because the external teacher provides only text, the same training procedure applies to sharedtokenizer, cross-tokenizer, and closed API teachers. We evaluate BSD under three forms of teacher access: (1) shared-tokenizer, (2) cross-tokenizer, and (3) closed API teachers. Across twelve teacher student pairs and three math reasoning benchmarks, BSD remains effective in all three settings while avoiding the severe degradation that SFT exhibits in several pairs. Our contributions are as follows: We introduce BSD, unified on-policy distillation framework that turns reasoning traces from external teachers into token-level guidance through privileged self-teacher. We evaluate BSD across twelve teacher student pairs spanning shared-tokenizer, crosstokenizer, and closed API teachers, demonstrating that BSD generally outperforms the baselines across all three settings. Our analyses show that BSD maintains stable training, benefits from more complete reasoning traces, and concentrates its guidance on uncertain tokens, with stronger guidance associated with larger performance gains.

sections.title: 3 Bridged Self-Distillation
sections.content: To distill from teacher models with different tokenizers or text-only access, we need guidance that does not depend on their token probabilities. Directly imitating stronger teachers reasoning can also be difficult for smaller student. We therefore propose Bridged Self-Distillation (BSD), which only needs teachers reasoning trace and turns it into guidance on the students own rollouts (Figure 2). We describe the key components below.

sections.content: Benchmarks. We evaluate on three competitionlevel mathematics benchmarks: AIME 2024 (Mathematical Association of America, 2024), AIME 2025 (Mathematical Association of America, 2025), and HMMT 2025 (Dekoninck et al., 2026). sections.title: 4.4 Baselines
sections.content: We consider the following baselines, which use the same backbones and training problems as BSD. Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). We train each student to imitate the external teachers reasoning traces (Kim and Rush, 2016) using the same traces that serve as privileged context for BSD. Vanilla OPD. For the shared-tokenizer teacher, we use standard OPD (Lu and Lab, 2025), which is optimized by minimizing the log-probability differences between student and teacher. Cross-Tokenizer OPD (xOPD). For the crosstokenizer teacher, we use cross-tokenizer OPD (Niu et al., 2026), denoted xOPD, which aligns the two tokenizations and maps teacher token logprobabilities onto student tokens. Rubric-Based OPD (ROPD). For the closed API teacher, we use ROPD (Fang et al., 2026), which asks the teacher to derive rubric for each question and score the students rollouts against it.

sections.title: 5.1 Comparing Teacher Access
sections.content: BSD consistently improves over the base model and outperforms the distillation baselines across teacher settings. Table 1 reports Avg@4 for four students paired with shared-tokenizer, crosstokenizer, and closed API teachers. BSD improves over the base model in all twelve teacherstudent pairs, with gains of 1.2 to 4.7 points, and achieves the best average score in eleven pairs. Shared-tokenizer teacher. Qwen3-32B shares the students tokenizer, allowing vanilla OPD to score their rollouts directly with teacher token probabilities. BSD outperforms SFT for all four students by 3.3 to 8.6 points in average score, while SFT falls below the base model for three of them. Thus, even within the same model family, directly imitating much stronger teachers reasoning can be difficult for smaller students (Zhang et al., 2023, 2025). BSD also matches or outperforms vanilla OPD for every student: the two tie in average score for Qwen3-1.7B, and BSD scores up to 3.6 points higher for the other three. This indicates that sharing tokenizer does not ensure compatible reasoning patterns between distinct models, which prior work identifies as important for successful OPD (Li et al., 2026b). BSD instead uses self-teacher, copy of the student conditioned on the external teachers reasoning, so that the token-level guidance comes from the students own model and is therefore more compatible. Cross-tokenizer teacher. Because the teacher model Nemotron-3-30B-A3B uses different tokenizer from the students, xOPD must align the two tokenizations and map the teachers token probabilities onto the students tokens. Nevertheless, xOPD does not yield consistent gains over the base models. It improves the average score of Qwen3-0.6B by 3.4 points, but brings only marginal gains of 0.5 and 0.6 points for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-4B-Instruct, respectively, and decreases the score of Qwen3-1.7B by 0.8 points. This indicates that constructing mapping makes cross-tokenizer OPD possible, but does not guarantee effective token-level supervision. In contrast, BSD improves all four base models by 1.2 to 4.4 points and outperforms xOPD for three of the four students, with Qwen3-0.6B as the only exception. BSD therefore provides strong alternative for cross-tokenizer distillation, obtaining guidance directly in the students token space without mappings between distinct vocabularies. Closed API teacher. GPT-5.6 Luna is accessible only through text API and exposes neither token probabilities nor its tokenizer. Moreover, it returns short final responses averaging 247 tokens, compared with about 4,000 tokens from the other two teachers. Directly using these responses as SFT targets causes the students to imitate their length (cf. Section 5.2). Consequently, SFT falls below the base model for three of the four students, with Qwen3-0.6B dropping from 10.8 to 2.8. sections.content: We further examine how distillation changes the students throughout training. Figure 3 tracks two aspects of this progression: response length across all twelve teacherstudent pairs and benchmark performance in representative closed API setting.2 Response length. Figure 3ac shows that the effect of SFT on response length depends strongly on the external teacher. With the shared-tokenizer teacher, response lengths remain largely stable for all methods. With the cross-tokenizer teacher, BSD and xOPD remain stable, whereas SFT usually increases the response lengths, most notably for Qwen3-1.7B. The most pronounced shift occurs with the closed API teacher, whose responses average only 247 tokens. SFT trains directly on these short responses, causing all four students to gradually shorten their outputs. In contrast, BSD and the corresponding OPD baselines maintain relatively stable response lengths across all twelve pairs. These trends show that using the external teachers reasoning trace as privileged context allows BSD to preserve the students output form without forcing it to reproduce the traces length. 2More performance curves for other teacherstudent pairs are provided in Appendix H, where SFT performance also frequently deteriorates over training. Figure 3d illustrates this behavior for Qwen3-4B-Instruct distilled from GPT-5.6 Luna. SFT is already below the base model at the beginning, and its performance falls to nearly zero by the end of training. The additional curves in Appendix show similar collapses or declines of SFT in other teacherstudent pairs. These results further indicate that directly imitating stronger teachers reasoning traces can lead to unstable training. In contrast, ROPD and BSD maintain stable or slightly improving performance throughout training. BSD is particularly notable because it uses the same external-teacher reasoning traces as SFT, but treats them as privileged context to guide the students own rollouts rather than as targets to imitate. Appendix further shows that SFT suffers from catastrophic forgetting on two out-ofdomain benchmarks, whereas BSD does not.

sections.title: 6.2 What the Token-Level Guidance Captures
sections.content: BSD uses the token-level guidance δt to distribute verifier feedback across the tokens of an unsuccessful rollout. To understand this signal, we examine which tokens it emphasizes, whether its strength is associated with BSDs gains, and how it affects the students behavior. Table 2 reports the quantitative results averaged across teachers, with the measurement setup described in Appendix A, while Figure 5 illustrates concrete example. Guidance targets uncertain tokens and tracks performance gains. The correlation ρH between per-token guidance magnitude and the students token entropy on unsuccessful rollouts ranges 7 from 0.83 to 0.90, indicating that the strongest guidance concentrates on tokens where the student is most uncertain. Its magnitude also follows the gains: Qwen3-4B-Instruct has both the weakest guidance and the smallest gain, whereas Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B receive stronger guidance and achieve larger gains. Thus, BSD achieves larger gains when the privileged context more strongly changes the students predictions, particularly at uncertain tokens. Case study: BSD encourages self-correction. Figure 5 shows an AIME24 problem where the base Qwen3-4B finds the correct integer = 5694 but misreads its quotient and remainder when it is divided by 1000. Given the same prefix containing this mistake, the base model continues without revisiting the division, whereas the student trained with BSD re-checks the step, identifies the error, and reaches the correct answer. Across eight continuations from this prefix, the BSD student solves the problem six times, compared with four for the base model. This example illustrates how BSD can help the student revisit and correct an uncertain intermediate step rather than persist with an initially plausible but incorrect rollout.

sections.title: 7 Related Work
sections.content: Knowledge distillation. Knowledge distillation transfers supervision from stronger teacher to smaller student through output distributions or generated sequences (Hinton et al., 2015; Kim and Rush, 2016). For reasoning models, this idea is commonly instantiated by training on teachergenerated reasoning traces, although large teacher student gaps can make direct imitation difficult (Shridhar et al., 2023; Hsieh et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2026; Lyu et al., 2026). On-policy distillation instead learns from studentgenerated rollouts under token-level teacher guidance (Gu et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026b). Recent variants extend OPD to heterogeneous tokenizers (Minixhofer et al., 2025; Boizard et al., 2025; Niu et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026) and black-box teachers (Ye et al., 2026a; Xiong et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026), but typically require setting-specific supervision. In contrast, BSD offers an effective and unified framework for all these settings. Learning with privileged information provides general framework for exploiting supervision that is available only during training, with generalized distillation connecting this idea to teacherstudent learning (Vapnik and Vashist, 2009; Lopez-Paz et al., 2016). In language models, context distillation instantiates this principle by internalizing information from instructions, demonstrations, or other contextual signals into model that later operates without them (Snell et al., 2022; Shin et al., 2025; Duan et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2026b). Recent self-distillation methods further use the model itself as privileged teacher by conditioning it on answers, solutions, feedback, or successful trajectories (Zhao et al., 2026; Penaloza et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026b; Ding, 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a; Pan et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a; Kim et al., 2026). BSD follows this privileged paradigm, but uses reasoning from an external teacher as the privileged context.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: 3Appendix further compares the wording of responses from the base model and the BSD-trained student, and Appendix shows an example of the token-level guidance under the trace and under the answer. We introduced BSD, unified framework for distilling from any teacher that provides reasoning traces. BSD uses the external teachers reason8 ing trace as privileged context for self-teacher, producing compatible token-level guidance in the students own token space without teacher probabilities or vocabulary mappings. Across twelve teacherstudent pairs spanning shared-tokenizer, cross-tokenizer, and closed API settings, BSD improves every base model and achieves the best or tied average performance among the distillation methods in eleven pairs. Our analyses further show that BSD supports stable training, benefits from more complete reasoning, and focuses its guidance on uncertain tokens, establishing reasoning traces as common and effective interface for on-policy distillation.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: We evaluate BSD with shared-tokenizer, crosstokenizer, and closed API teachers across twelve teacherstudent pairs and analyze its token-level guidance. However, we acknowledge three main limitations. First, due to computational constraints, our experiments are limited to students of up to 4B parameters from one model family and to English competition mathematics. Future work could examine whether the gains of BSD hold for larger students, other model families, and other domains. Second, BSD relies on verifier to set the direction of each update, so it applies only to tasks whose answers can be checked automatically and not to open-ended ones. Whether the agreement between the student and the external teacher can serve as verifier in such tasks remains to be explored. Finally, our analysis relates the token-level guidance to the gains of BSD only through correlations across students. It characterizes where the guidance concentrates but does not establish which tokens it helps, or why, which we leave for future work.

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: This work fine-tunes publicly released language models on publicly available mathematical reasoning datasets and evaluates them with automatic verifiers. It involves no human subjects, no personally identifiable information, and no newly collected data. The method transfers reasoning capability that the teacher models already expose through their public interfaces, so we do not identify risks beyond those general to improving open-weight reasoning models.

The students trained with these responses serve only to study distillation methods: we do not deploy them, offer them as service, or use them to develop models that compete with the API provider. sections.title: A Experimental Details
sections.content: Teacher traces. Teacher traces are generated once, before training, with the settings in Table 3 and the prompts in Appendix B. For closed teacher that hides its reasoning, the trace is built from the response it returns: we enclose the derivation of the response in reasoning block (<think> and </think>) and place its boxed final answer after the block, which is the format of the students own responses. Within teacherstudent pair, BSD and SFT use the same traces, BSD as privileged context for the self-teacher and SFT as training targets. Training. Tables 4 and 5 give the training configuration. All methods train LoRA adapters (Hu et al., 2022), and the learning rate is warmed up linearly over the first 10 updates and is constant afterwards. Training sets are identical for all methods within teacherstudent pair. For BSD, the students score pt uses its current log-probabilities, and the rollouttrainer gap is corrected with tokenlevel truncated importance sampling (Yu et al., 2025). During training, BSD adds one forward pass of the self-teacher over the students rollouts. This pass takes 7 to 18 seconds per update, depending on the length of the trace, which is under 10% of the update time. The limit of 2,048 tokens on the prompt applies to the students prompt, which contains only the question. The self-teachers prompt also contains the trace and has separate limit of 12,288 tokens. The longest question and trace together take 8,950 tokens, so no trace is truncated in any run; the hint and guide of Section 6.1 are shorter than the full trace. In total, the training, evaluation, and Compute. ablation runs reported in this paper take about 1,450 GPU-hours on NVIDIA H100 and H200 GPUs. Table 6 reports the GPU-hours of training with each method for the Qwen3-4B student, measured on NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The values cover the 150 updates and exclude checkpoint saving, checkpoint evaluation, and the generation of the teacher traces before training. OPD and xOPD keep the teacher on one additional GPU during training, which is counted, and ROPD queries the teacher through its API, whose compute is not counted. Evaluation. Table 7 gives the evaluation parameters. Checkpoints are selected on the development set, and the earliest checkpoint is taken in case of tie. Each of the three benchmarks contains 30 problems. Final answers are checked with MathVerify.4 Guidance measurement. For Table 2, each student generates six rollouts for each of 24 hard problems shared by all students before training, and each rollout is scored under one verified trace from each of the three teachers. We write δ for the mean of the signed guidance δt over all tokens of the unsuccessful rollouts, and Table 2 reports its absolute value δ. sections.title: B Prompt Templates
sections.content: All prompts are given as the user message of the models chat template. For Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-1.7B, and Qwen3-0.6B, is prompted with the question: the student Problem: {question x} Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within boxed{}. The self-teacher receives the same question together with the external teachers trace: Problem: {question x} Here is reference solution to this problem: <reference_solution> {trace z} </reference_solution> After reading the reference solution above, make sure you truly understand the reasoning behind each step do not copy or paraphrase it. Now, using your own words and independent reasoning, derive the same final answer to the problem above. Think step by step, explore different approaches, and dont be afraid to backtrack or reconsider if something doesnt work out: Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within boxed{}. For Qwen3-4B-Instruct, template opens the reasoning block (<think>) at the start of the response, and the last line of both prompts is additionally replaced by: the chat Think through the problem step by step inside <think> and </think> tags. After </think>, give your final solution and put the final answer within boxed{}. The token-level guidance is computed on the students original response tokens appended after each prompt; responses are not decoded and retokenized. Teacher traces. All three external teachers generate their traces from the same prompt: Problem: {question x} Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within boxed{}. RLSD ablation. For RLSD (Section 6.1), the self-teacher receives the ground-truth answer in place of the trace: Problem: {question x} Here is verified correct final answer to this problem: <reference_solution> {answer} </reference_solution> After reading the reference solution above, make sure you truly understand the reasoning behind each step do not copy or paraphrase it. Now, using your own words and independent reasoning, derive the same final answer to the problem above. Think step by step, explore different approaches, and dont be afraid to backtrack or reconsider if something doesnt work out: Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within boxed{}. Guide and hint ablations. For the ablation on the form of the privileged context (Section 6.1), the external teacher rewrites its trace as guide or as hint. The guide is generated with: You are helping student who is stuck on math problem. Below are the problem and worked reasoning trace written by stronger solver. 15 Problem: {question x} Worked reasoning: {trace z} Write step-by-step guide for the student: numbered list of the steps of the solution, in order, at most 8 steps and under 150 words in total. Rules: each step says what to do and why (the idea, the quantity to set up, the case split), without carrying out the computation; do not state the final answer; do not give intermediate numerical results; do not restate the problem; plain text, no markdown formatting. Output only the numbered list. The hint is generated with the same opening, problem, and worked reasoning, followed by this instruction: Write hint of at most three sentences (under 80 words) that points the student to the key idea or the first decisive step. Rules: do not state the final answer; do not give numerical intermediate results; do not write out the solution; name the method or the observation that unlocks the problem. Output only the hint. The self-teacher then receives the guide, with the verified final answer appended, in place of the reference solution: Problem: {question x} Here is step-by-step guide to this problem, followed by its verified final answer: <guide> {guide} </guide> After reading the guide above, make sure you truly understand why each step is needed do not copy or paraphrase it. Now, using your own words and independent reasoning, carry out the steps and derive the same final answer to the problem above. Think step by step, explore different approaches, and dont be afraid to backtrack or reconsider if something doesnt work out: Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within boxed{}. The self-teacher prompt for the hint is: Problem: {question x} Here is hint for this problem, followed by its verified final answer: <hint> {hint} </hint> After reading the hint above, make sure you truly understand the idea it points to do not copy or paraphrase it. Now, using your own words and independent reasoning, work out the solution and derive the same final answer to the problem above. Think step by step, explore different approaches, and dont be afraid to backtrack or reconsider if something doesnt work out: Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within boxed{}.

sections.title: Responses
sections.content: The case study in Section 6.2 shows single response. Here we compare the wording of responses across the three benchmarks, for the base Qwen3-4B and the student trained with BSD on Qwen3-32B traces, with four samples per problem from each model. On 26 problems the base model gives at least one incorrect response and the BSD student at least one correct response; these comprise 45 incorrect responses of the base model and 69 correct responses of the BSD student. For every word n-gram with 3 that is frequent in these responses (1,508 n-grams), we compute its rate per 1,000 words in the two groups for each problem and paired t-statistic over the problems. The rates of 24 n-grams differ with > 3, where about four are expected by chance; Table 12 lists examples. Incorrect responses of the base model contain more expressions of negation and doubt, and correct responses of the BSD student more expressions of verification. The correct responses are also shorter, with 19,057 tokens on average against 24,279. This comparison changes the model and the correctness of the response at the same time, so the differences cannot be attributed to BSD alone. We report them as description of the two groups of responses and not as independent evidence that BSD induces self-correction.

sections.title: Results
sections.content: Figure 8 shows the score trend for three further settings, in the format of Figure 3d. In each of them the score of SFT declines over training, while BSD stays stable. Out-of-Domain Evaluation To examine how the distillation methods affect outof-domain performance, we evaluate the Qwen3-4B student on general knowledge and legal questions, at every saved checkpoint of BSD, SFT, and the OPD variant of each teacher. We use two sets of 200 multiple-choice questions: from MMLUPro (Wang et al., 2024), 20 questions from each of its ten categories other than mathematics, physics, chemistry, and engineering, and from LEXam (Fan et al., 2026), 200 four-choice questions in English and German, sampled in the proportion of the two languages in the benchmark. The protocol is that of Table 7, and the base model scores 63.5 on the MMLU-Pro questions and 45.9 on the LEXam questions. Figure 9 shows that SFT is unstable during training, whereas BSD and the OPD variants are not. On the MMLU-Pro questions, SFT with GPT-5.6 Luna falls steadily from 62.1 at step 25 to 54.1 at step 150, 9.4 points below the base model, and SFT with Nemotron-3-30B-A3B falls from 64.0 to 60.8. On the LEXam questions, SFT with GPT-5.6 falls to 40.5 at step 100, 5.4 points below the base model. Under bootstrap paired over questions, these three differences from the base model exclude zero at the 95% level, whereas no difference of SFT with Qwen3-32B does. In contrast, at every checkpoint and for all three teachers, BSD and the OPD variants are never more than 1.1 points below the base model on the MMLU-Pro questions and 3.5 points on the LEXam questions. Learning from the students own rollouts therefore preserves its abilities outside the training domain, whereas imitating the teachers reasoning traces can erase them.
